## Question 1
vector_age<- c(15, 28, 32, 36, 27, 18, 52, 39, 42, 29, 35, 31, 27, 22, 37, 34, 19, 20, 57, 49, 50, 37, 46, 25, 17, 12, 42, 53, 41, 51, 35, 24, 33, 8)

#A. How many data points?
length(vector_age)

#B. Find the reciprocal of age
1 / vector_age

#C. Assign also new_age <-c(age, o, age). what happens to new_age?
new_age <- c(vector_age, 0, vector_age)
#it combines the age,  the number 0, and age again into one singular vector.

#D. Find the minimum and the maximum value of age.
min(vector_age)
max(vector_age)

##Question 2 rep(c("A","B"), each = 2) and rep(c("A","B"), times = 2) both produce a vector of length 4, but with different element orders.
#explain in your own words

##each = 2: Repeats each individual element of the vector a specified number of times consecutively before moving on to the next element. For c("A", "B"), it repeats "A" twice, then "B" twice, resulting in "A", "A", "B", "B".

## times = 2: Repeats the entire vector as a whole the specified number of times. For c("A", "B"), it takes the complete sequence and duplicates it, resulting in "A", "B", "A", "B".

##Question 3 Compare seq(1, 20, by = 2) with seq(1, 20, length.out = 5). What does each argument (by vs length.out) control, and when would you use one over the other in a real analysis?
#- the by controls the exact distance/increment between consecutive elements in the vector, meanwhile the length.out controls the total amount of items the final vector will contain,automatically calculating the step size to fit that exact count.

## Question 4 
vec_num <- seq(20, 60)

mean(vec_num)

sum(vec_num)

length(vec_num)
